texts.cpp.arrays.theory:
An array stores a sequence of elements of the same type. For three integers, you can write int data[3] = {4, 7, 2};. The indices are 0, 1 and 2. In modern code, std::array<int, 3> data = {4, 7, 2}; from <array> is convenient for a fixed size. It provides size(), access with [] and range-based for iteration.

[] does not check bounds: an ordinary element's index must be strictly less than the size. data.at(index) checks the bound and throws std::out_of_range if it is violated; exception handling comes later, and these tasks guarantee valid indices. To read three values into an array, use an index-based loop. Changing a copy in range for does not change the array element; use data[i] for writing.

In standard C++, a built-in array's size must be a valid constant expression, not an arbitrary n read from cin. For an input-dependent size, use vector.

int energy = 20; creates an object with an initial value. energy = 12; changes an existing object. Assignment evaluates the right-hand side first, then stores the result on the left: energy = energy + 5; adds 5 to the previous value. It is not a mathematical equality.

The shorthand energy += 5; does the same for our integer variable. The operators -= and *= work similarly. After assignment, the old value is lost unless you saved it elsewhere. To exchange values, use a temporary variable: int saved = a; a = b; b = saved;. Names must start with a letter or underscore; for these exercises, choose clear Latin-letter names and avoid reserved naming patterns.

texts.cpp.branches.theory:
An if / else if / else chain checks conditions from top to bottom and executes only the first matching branch. Unlike independent if statements, it prevents repeated output. Start with conditions that must not be hidden by broader ones.

switch (code) selects a case label using an integer or character value. break exits the switch; without it, execution may continue into the following case. default handles other values. Use if for ranges and compound logic, and switch for individual codes. Here, break exits switch; its role in loops will be studied separately.

texts.cpp.characters.theory:
The loop for (char ch : text) iterates over a string's elements by value. The variable ch is a copy of the current char; changing ch does not change text. To build a result, create an empty std::string result and append suitable characters using result += ch;. This is a range-based for loop: it traverses an existing sequence without a manual index.

In this lesson, input is restricted to ASCII: Latin letters, digits and spaces. Test for a digit using '0' <= ch && ch <= '9'. The standard guarantees consecutive codes for decimal digits; ch - '0' gives a digit's numeric value. Do not generalize letter ranges to every encoding and language. A direct comparison ch == 'a' checks for that specific character.

texts.cpp.conversion.theory:
An operation's result type is determined by its operands, not by the destination variable. double x = 5 / 2; stores 2.0 because integer division has already happened. Writing 5.0 / 2 or static_cast<double>(a) / b performs floating-point division. static_cast<double>(a) explicitly converts the value of a.

Converting double to int discards the fractional part towards zero, but is valid only when the resulting value is representable. Parentheses and casts must come before an operation that would lose the information you need. Do not conclude that double is always the most accurate type: different types have different purposes and limitations. The small integers in these tasks convert exactly to double.

texts.cpp.division.theory:
When both operands are integers, / performs integer division: 17 / 5 gives 3. The remainder operator % complements that division: 17 % 5 gives 2. For nonnegative a and positive b, a = (a / b) * b + a % b, and the remainder is between 0 and b-1.

For negative integers, the quotient is truncated towards zero: -17 / 5 is -3, and -17 % 5 is -2. This is not rounding down. Our packaging tasks use nonnegative numbers, so the everyday interpretation of a remainder applies. Neither / nor % may use a zero divisor. When a divisor is read, the task guarantees that it is positive.

A // comment continues to the end of the source line and is not executed. A /* ... */ comment can span several lines. Inside quotation marks, // is just text. Do not hide the only required statements inside a comment.

texts.cpp.first.theory:
An algorithm is a finite sequence of steps that an executor can follow. A program expresses an algorithm in a programming language. C++ is case-sensitive: main and Main are different names.

An ordinary console program starts executing in int main(). Braces enclose its body. The statement std::cout << "Ready"; sends text to standard output. A semicolon ends the statement; quotation marks delimit the text and are not printed. The directive #include <iostream> makes input/output declarations available. For now, use this structure without trying to memorize every detail.

In codelib, you can write code, save it and compare it with a reference solution. There is no built-in execution yet. Do not confuse marking a task complete yourself with checking a program using a compiler.

texts.cpp.flow.theory:
break exits the nearest loop or switch. continue skips the remainder of the current iteration: in for, the step executes next, followed by the condition; in while, the condition is checked immediately. A misplaced continue can skip a while counter update and create an infinite loop.

In nested loops, the inner loop runs through its iterations for each outer value. For a table of rows lines and cols characters, the outer loop handles lines and the inner loop handles each line's contents. Print the newline after the inner loop.

When streaming a known number of values, do not stop reading early without a reason: if more data is needed afterwards, the unread values remain in the input stream.

texts.cpp.for.theory:
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { ... } creates a counter i, tests the condition before each iteration, and increments i after the body. With n=3, the body sees i equal to 0, 1 and 2. ++i increments the variable by one. For now, use increment as a separate step rather than inside complex expressions.

If the condition is false initially, the body executes zero times. A variable declared in the for header is available inside the loop, but not after it. To accumulate a sum, create sum=0 before the loop and add values inside. Do not reset sum on every iteration.

Plan output separators separately: if (i > 0) before a space can avoid a trailing space.

texts.cpp.functions.theory:
A function groups statements under a name. int square(int value) { return value * value; } takes one int and returns an int. The call square(4) evaluates the argument 4, passes it to the parameter value and obtains the result 16. A parameter is a name inside the function; an argument is a value at the call site.

return ends the current function and passes its result to the caller. A returned value is not printed by itself: you must store or print it. Functions that return an ordinary value must return it on every execution path. void denotes a function with no return value.

In this lesson, declare functions before main so their names are already known at each call. Do not try to define one ordinary function inside another.

texts.cpp.getline.theory:
std::getline(std::cin, line) reads text up to the end of a line, preserves spaces within it, and removes the terminating newline delimiter from the result. An empty input line produces an empty std::string. If you read a number with >> before getline, the newline at the end of its line normally remains in the input stream. The first getline may then read just that empty remainder.

When the format says 'a number on a separate line, then text', you can discard the rest of the number's line: std::cin.ignore(std::numeric_limits<std::streamsize>::max(), '\n');. Include <limits> for this. It deliberately removes everything up to the end of the first line. Do not apply it blindly when useful text is on the same line.

std::ws before getline discards all leading whitespace and empty lines; it is not a universal replacement when they matter.

texts.cpp.input.theory:
A variable is a named object that stores a value of a particular type. int count = 0; creates an integer variable named count with the initial value 0. Names are case-sensitive. std::cin >> count; reads an integer from standard input and stores it in count. You can read several numbers in a chain: std::cin >> price >> count;. Spaces and line breaks separate the numbers.

Do not use quotation marks when printing a variable: std::cout << count;. Writing "count" would print the word. The operators + and * add and multiply numbers. In this section, input is guaranteed to be valid and all results fit in int; we will study invalid input later. Do not print prompts such as "Enter a number" when the required output contains only the answer.

texts.cpp.searchvector.theory:
Linear search checks elements one by one. To find the first position, keep index=-1 when nothing has been found, then store i at the first match. In this model, real positions run from 0 to n-1, so −1 cannot be confused with one. After the search, do not use values[index] until you have checked index!=-1.

To change every element, use an index-based loop: values[i] += bonus;. A range for with int value would change only a copy. Equal values may occur many times: decide in advance whether you need the first match, the last, or all matches.

Do not add or remove container elements during an ordinary range for over that container: structural changes may invalidate the traversal. Here, filter into a separate result or change only existing elements' values.

texts.cpp.telemetry.theory:
You do not need to store every sequence in full. A sum needs an accumulator, a maximum needs the best value so far, and a count of rises needs the preceding measurement. These are streaming algorithms: read a new value, update the state, and move on.

Initialize the maximum of a nonempty sequence from its first value, not from zero: when every number is negative, zero is not their maximum. Compare adjacent measurements starting with the second one. The n≥1 contract makes it safe to read the first element separately.

The final task uses long long for the sum and floating-point division for the average.

double stores numbers with a fractional part: double distance = 2.5;. In C++ source, use a dot as the decimal separator. int stores integers; converting double to int discards the fractional part towards zero, provided that the result is representable.

char marker = 'A'; stores one character code unit written in single quotation marks; "A" is a string literal, not a char. A Russian character usually occupies several bytes in UTF-8, so one char cannot be promised to hold any letter. bool ready = true; stores true or false. Without special formatting, printing a bool produces 1 or 0.

For a fixed number of decimal places, include <iomanip> and output std::fixed << std::setprecision(2). This changes stream formatting, not the stored number. Valid numeric input in these tasks uses a decimal dot.

std::vector<int> values(n); from <vector> creates n integer elements initialized to zero. Here, n may be read from input. values.size() returns the current size. values.push_back(x) appends an element and increases the size. An empty vector has no elements; values.empty() checks for this.

To read n numbers, create a vector of size n and access values[i] for i from 0 to n-1. For an unknown number of additions, start with std::vector<int> values; and call push_back. Do not confuse size with reserved capacity: elements exist only within size().

You can calculate a sum as a stream, but a vector is useful when you need the data again, in a different order, or after computing an overall property.

texts.cpp.while.theory:
while (condition) { ... } tests its condition before every iteration. It is useful when the repetition count is not known in advance. The body must change the state that controls continuation; otherwise the loop may run forever.

To process the digits of a positive n, take n%10 and remove the last digit using n/=10. The /= operator assigns the quotient back to the variable. Zero needs attention: while(n>0) does not execute for it. do { ... } while (condition); tests the condition after the body and executes at least once. This form requires a semicolon after while.

long long holds the larger integers used in these tasks; initial values and bounds must still be specified.
